questions.q: What is the protagonist's name and his professional status at the start of the excerpt?
questions.a: The protagonist is Andrew Manson, a newly qualified doctor working as an assistant to Dr. Edward Page in Blaenelly. A wrong answer (e.g., naming Joe Morgan or Dr. Page) reveals the student cannot distinguish the central character from supporting characters, indicating a basic comprehension gap.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Andrew feels "resentful and confused" while waiting in the kitchen.
questions.a: Andrew is torn between his rational observation that marriages around him (Bramwell, Page, Denny) are failures and his emotional conviction that his love for Christine is ideal. A wrong answer that only lists the failed marriages misses the internal conflict between "level, doubting mind" and "overflowing heart," showing the student cannot infer psychological complexity from textual clues.

questions.q: Identify the specific medical technique Andrew uses to resuscitate the stillborn child and explain why he chooses it.
questions.a: Andrew uses alternating hot and cold water immersion (a "special method of respiration" recalled from a Samaritan case) to stimulate the asphyxiated infant. He chooses it because the child shows pallida (whiteness from asphyxia), and his "unnaturally tense" mind retrieves this specific treatment. A wrong answer citing generic CPR or injections shows the student cannot apply textual details to a practical medical decision.

questions.q: Compare Andrew's attitude toward the child at three moments: when the child is born lifeless, during the fifteen-minute resuscitation, and after the first cry.
questions.a: Initially, Andrew feels a "shiver of horror" and hesitation; during resuscitation, he persists with "desperate sense of defeat" yet refuses to quit; finally, the cry makes him "weak and dazed" with an "exquisite" sense of life. A wrong answer that treats his attitude as static (e.g., "he always wanted to save it") fails to track the emotional arc from professional dilemma to personal triumph.

questions.q: Evaluate whether Andrew's final statement "I've done something real at last" refers only to the medical success or also to a personal validation. Justify with evidence.
questions.a: It signifies both: medically, he saved two lives; personally, it validates his choice of profession over his doubts. The phrase "oblivious to all other work he had done in Blaenelly" shows previous work felt unreal. A wrong answer limiting it to medical success ignores the autobiographical undertone (Cronin's own medical career) and the thematic contrast between textbook medicine and lived practice.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from Andrew's perspective that night, capturing his inner shift from the kitchen reverie to the scullery realization.
questions.a: A strong entry mirrors the text's movement: starts with Christine's eyes and failed marriages, includes the midwife's "stillborn" whisper, the hot-cold water frenzy, and ends with the baby's cry and the thought "something real." A weak entry summarizes plot without voice or omits the internal conflict, showing inability to synthesize character perspective.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of the protagonist involves examining the central character's personality traits, internal conflicts, motivations, and development through their actions, thoughts, speech, and ______, using textual evidence to support inferences about their role in advancing the narrative's themes.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a doctor on call at 3 a.m., ______ and doubting your career choice, when a crisis forces you to act without thinking.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a doctor on call at ______ a.m., exhausted and doubting your career choice, when a crisis forces you to act without thinking.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must write a structured PEEL-paragraph analysis of Andrew Manson that integrates at least three textual evidences (actions, internal monologue, dialogue) to explain his transformation from disillusionment to professional fulfillment, linking it to the story's central theme of "doing something real.".
